Stoicism is a Hellenistic and Roman philosophy teaching that virtue is the highest good and the path to a fulfilling life. Founded in Athens by Zeno of Citium around three hundred before Christ, Stoicism holds that external events—wealth, health, reputation—are fundamentally indifferent; what matters is conforming one's will and judgment to reason and universal nature. By accepting what cannot be controlled and focusing effort on virtue, duty, and rational choice, the Stoic achieves ataraxia, mental tranquility, and apatheia, freedom from destructive emotion. The philosophy dominated Roman intellectual life and profoundly influenced Christianity, modern cognitive therapy, and secular ethics.

Stoicism was founded by Zeno of Citium around three hundred before Christ and developed by thinkers like Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius. The central claim is that virtue, living according to reason and nature, is the only true good; all else such as health, wealth, and fame is merely preferred indifferent. The universe operates via logos, a divine rational principle, and human reason is a fragment of this cosmic reason.

The Stoic approach to ethics and practice rests on a dichotomy of control: distinguish firmly between what lies in your control—your judgment, choice, and desire—and what does not, such as your body, property, and reputation. Through apatheia and ataraxia, freedom from destructive passion and mental disturbance, the Stoic achieves tranquility through rational acceptance and duty. This duty extends to oneself, family, society, and the cosmos, and virtue expresses itself through action aligned with reason and nature.

Stoicism's influence on history has been profound. The philosophy dominated Roman elite philosophy, and the Meditations by the emperor Marcus Aurelius is the canonical surviving Stoic text. Epictetus, formerly a slave, taught that inner freedom transcends external circumstance, a radical claim that influenced Christian and modern thought. The core insight—that suffering arises from irrational judgment rather than events themselves—anticipates modern Cognitive Behavioral Therapy. Stoicism emerged as a response to the loss of Greek city-state autonomy after Alexander's conquests, offering individuals a path to freedom and meaning independent of political circumstance. It shaped Roman law with its emphasis on natural justice, Christian virtue ethics especially asceticism and duty, and modern secular psychology through cognitive behavioral therapy, which borrows the Stoic insight that irrational impressions corrupt judgment.
